cards.grammarNote: The **preterite** is the narrative past — a single, completed action seen as finished. Regular **-ar** verbs take the endings **-é, -aste, -ó, -amos, -aron**. Only **yo** and **él/ella** carry a written accent.
cards.englishPhrase: Yesterday I worked at the office.

table.title: Preterite: -ar verbs (trabajar)
table.note: Accents only on trabajé and trabajó.

cards.grammarNote: **-er** and **-ir** verbs share the *same* preterite endings: **-í, -iste, -ió, -imos, -ieron**. So comer and vivir conjugate identically.
cards.englishPhrase: Last night I ate at the restaurant.

table.title: Preterite: -er / -ir (comer, vivir)
table.note: -er and -ir are identical in the preterite.

cards.grammarNote: For a finished, one-time action use the preterite. The **él/ella** form of an -ar verb ends in **-ó** (cocinó), never the present **-a** (cocina).

cards.english: I went to the park. (ir → fui)
cards.grammarNote: **ser** and **ir** have the *same* irregular preterite: **fui, fuiste, fue, fuimos, fueron** — context tells them apart. **Fui al parque** = I went; **fui médico** = I was a doctor.
cards.englishPhrase: Yesterday I went to the park.

cards.english: I was at home last night. (estar → estuve)
cards.grammarNote: A group of irregulars takes a new stem + the endings **-e, -iste, -o, -imos, -ieron** (no accents): **estar→estuv-, tener→tuv-, poder→pud-**. So: estuve, tuve, pude.
cards.englishPhrase: Last night I was at home.

cards.grammarNote: More irregular stems, same **-e/-o** endings: **hacer→hic-** (but **hizo** with z), **decir→dij-** (dijeron, no i), **venir→vin-**.

table.title: Irregular preterite (hacer, decir, venir)
table.note: hizo spelled with z; dijeron drops the i.

cards.english: Say the preterite 'yo' form. (I ate / drank / lived)
cards.grammarNote: The **yo** preterite of regular -er/-ir verbs ends in a stressed **-í**: comer→comí, beber→bebí, vivir→viví.
cards.englishPhrase: I ate, I drank, I lived.

produce.concept: Preterite = one finished action in the past
produce.task: I ate, I drank, I lived

cards.english: As a child I used to swim. (imperfect, -ar)
cards.grammarNote: The **imperfect** is the 'used to / was ‑ing' past — habits and background, no clear end. Regular **-ar** verbs take **-aba, -abas, -aba, -ábamos, -aban**.
cards.englishPhrase: As a child I used to swim at the beach.
cards.phrase: De niño nadaba en la playa.

table.title: Imperfect: -ar verbs (nadar)
table.note: yo and él/ella are identical: nadaba.

cards.english: As a child I used to eat a lot of bread. (imperfect, -er/-ir)
cards.grammarNote: **-er** and **-ir** verbs share the imperfect endings **-ía, -ías, -ía, -íamos, -ían** — every form carries an accent on the **í**.
cards.englishPhrase: As a child I used to eat a lot of bread.

table.title: Imperfect: -er / -ir (comer, vivir)
table.note: Accent on every í. -er and -ir identical.

cards.english: As a child I was happy. (ser → era)
cards.grammarNote: The imperfect has only **three** irregular verbs: **ser→era, ir→iba, ver→veía**. Learn these; everything else is regular.
cards.englishPhrase: As a child I was happy.

cards.english: She always cooked at home. (habit → imperfect)
cards.grammarNote: Words like **siempre** (always) and **nunca** (never) signal a repeated habit → use the **imperfect** (cocinaba), not the preterite (cocinó).

cards.english: Say the imperfect. (I used to work / she used to study)
cards.grammarNote: Imperfect = 'used to' or 'would' (habitual). -ar yo/él ends in **-aba**: trabajaba, estudiaba.
cards.englishPhrase: I used to work, she used to study.

produce.concept: Imperfect = used to / would (a past habit)
produce.task: I used to work, she used to study

cards.english: I ate out — once vs. every day.
cards.grammarNote: Same verb, two pasts: **preterite** = one finished event; **imperfect** = a repeated habit or ongoing background. **Comí** (I ate, that once) vs **comía** (I used to eat).
cards.englishPhrase: Yesterday I ate out; as a child I ate at home.
cards.phrase: Ayer comí en el restaurante; de niño comía en casa.

cards.grammarNote: The time expression usually decides the tense. **ayer, anoche, la semana pasada** → a finished point → **preterite**. **siempre, de niño** → a habit → **imperfect**.
cards.englishPhrase: Yesterday I worked; as a child I worked here.

table.title: Which past does the time word want?
table.note: A fixed point → preterite; a habit → imperfect.

cards.english: I was cooking when she arrived. (background + event)
cards.grammarNote: For an interrupted scene, the ongoing background is **imperfect** (cocinaba) and the event that cuts in is **preterite** (llegó). English 'was ‑ing' → imperfect.
cards.englishPhrase: I was cooking when she arrived.

cloze.prompt: I was cooking (ongoing) when she arrived

cards.english: I arrived, cooked, and ate. (a chain of events)
cards.grammarNote: A sequence of completed actions, each moving the story forward, is all **preterite**: llegué, cociné, comí. (Note llegar → **llegué** keeps the hard g with -ué.)
cards.englishPhrase: I arrived, I cooked, and I ate.

produce.concept: A chain of finished actions → all preterite
produce.task: I arrived, I cooked, and I ate
produce.gloss: each completed step moves the story → preterite
